title: mamori.protection-scope/1
description: What was protected in one scope, carrying no protected value. See ADR 0032. Two invariants in the $comment below cannot be expressed here and must be enforced by the consumer; a third used to be there and is now in the schema itself.

contract.description: Frozen contract identifier. A consumer that does not recognise one must refuse the record rather than read the fields it happens to know. A record containing any surrogate declares '+surrogate' instead, so that a consumer written only for tokens refuses it through the check it already has, rather than through a rule it has to remember every time. Reading surrogate records is an opt-in, because knowing they exist is the whole of what makes them safe to read.

by.description: Producer, as name/version. The version matters: it says which rules and which placeholder grammar were in force.

scope.description: The scope the placeholders were allocated in, and the scope restoration needs. mamori generates 'session-' plus twelve hex characters of a random UUID, with no input from the document. A caller may supply its own, and then it is the caller's obligation to keep the document out of it -- an identifier derived from content moves the oracle problem from policy_hash to here. mamori refuses at protect time when a detected value occurs in the scope.

reversible.description: Whether every replacement can be undone. False when anything was masked: a mask has no mapping behind it. A consumer that does not find this property must read it as false -- a wrong true fails silently, and an honest quotation gets reported as a fabrication.

mode.description: A summary of how values were substituted, not a switch selecting which array to read. Surrogates are enabled per entity type, so one document routinely carries both. The contract identifier, not this field, is what stops a token-only consumer from reading half a record and believing it whole.

placeholders.description: Every value replaced by a token. Admissible because the token is in the protected text: a holder of that text recovers this list with one regular expression, so the record discloses nothing it did not already have. It is also what lets a consumer tell a token mamori minted from one the user typed.

protected.description: Every value replaced by a SURROGATE, as a kind and a count and never a string. The protected text deliberately does not announce these, so naming them would say which values are invented, by elimination which are real, and would mark the exact spans that held a real one.

masked.description: Every value replaced by a fixed mask, as a kind and a count. This is why 'reversible' may be false, and it is what tells a downstream which claims it can no longer check -- the difference between 'unsupported' and 'unverifiable'.

recall.description: The stance the detectors ran under. Absent means the producer did not know it, not that a default applied.

policy_hash.description: A fingerprint of the SETTINGS and of nothing else. It must be computed over the policy alone: a hash mixing in anything from the document turns this record into an oracle for confirming guesses about content.

$comment: Invariants JSON Schema 2020-12 cannot express, because it cannot compare two properties of the same object. (1) Every token in 'placeholders' occurs in the protected text; a record naming a token the body does not contain is describing a different document. (2) A record describes exactly ONE scope: placeholder numbering is unique only within one, so two scopes merged into a single record make <PERSON_001> ambiguous, and ambiguous in the direction that restores the wrong person's name. The third invariant this comment used to carry -- that a token-only consumer must refuse a record holding surrogates -- is now in the schema above, because splitting the contract identifier turned a comparison of two properties into a pair of discrete cases 'if'/'then' can state. FOR CONSUMERS WHO CANNOT RUN A VALIDATOR: the check that survives a version change is `protected` being non-empty, not the contract identifier. Records written before the identifier was split declared the plain contract while carrying surrogates, because there was nothing else to declare; a reader that keys on the identifier refuses those only from 0.27.0 onward, while a reader that refuses any record it cannot fully enumerate -- `protected` non-empty and no handling for it -- refuses both. The identifier ties the name to the contents; the non-emptiness ties the contents to what the reader can do with them, and only the second is a property of the record rather than of its vintage. Observed by iriguchi, whose reader accepted eight of nine malformed records including one that declared the plain contract and listed surrogate-protected values -- it reported a finding and dropped three surrogates in silence, which is the failure this contract exists to prevent.

allOf.$comment: The plain contract may not carry surrogates. Expressible because both sides are discrete: 'if' on a const, 'then' on a length.
And the +surrogate contract may not be used without one.
